title: The serve, explained: why table tennis's first shot has the strictest rule
description: Table tennis serve rules explained: the open palm, the 16cm toss and the hidden-serve ban, with a century of history and Eleven's count of close games.
standfirst: A Japanese player lost a game on two service faults in Istanbul last week. The rule that caught him has been rewritten again and again since 1926, each time to close a trick.
body: At 9-9 in the third game of his first-round match at [WTT Contender Istanbul](/news/wtt-contender-istanbul-2026-anna-hursey-hashimoto-li-tianyang-yokotani-faults.html) last Thursday, Jo Yokotani tossed the ball up to serve and heard the umpire call a fault. He served again and was faulted again, the second time, he said, before the ball had even reached his racket. Two points, no rally, game to China's Li Tianyang, who went on to win the match 3-1. Earlier in the match Yokotani had been warned that his serve could not be seen, and he had changed his action to comply.

"I could not understand by what criteria it was judged a fault," the 106th-ranked Japanese player wrote on social media afterwards (translated from Japanese). "On the world stage of WTT, I have serious doubts about players not receiving an explanation they can accept, and about officials not being able to communicate sufficiently."

It was a small match on a minor tour stop, and it went almost unnoticed outside Japan. Yet it touched the oldest running argument in table tennis. The table tennis serve is the one shot in the sport that a player hits entirely on their own terms, and for a century the rule-makers have been trying to stop it becoming unplayable. With WTT Star Contender Muscat under way this week, the Mixed Team World Cup starting on 29 November and the WTT Finals in Hong Kong from 8 December, the serve will decide more of the biggest points of the year than any other stroke. For anyone who has watched a highlight and wondered why players spend so long fiddling with the ball before they hit it, this is what is going on.
## What the rule says

Law 2.6 of the ITTF's Laws of Table Tennis runs to seven short clauses, and every one of them exists because somebody once found a way around the previous version. The serve must start with the ball "resting freely on the open palm of the server's stationary free hand": the free hand is the one without the racket, and it has to be flat and still, so that the ball cannot be flicked, gripped or spun. The server must then project the ball "near vertically upwards, without imparting spin", so that it rises at least 16cm after leaving the palm. That is a fraction higher than the net, which stands 15.25cm above the table, and the ball has to be struck on the way down.

Then comes geometry. From the moment the serve begins until the ball is hit, it must be above the level of the table and behind the server's end line. It must not be hidden from the receiver, the player waiting to return it, by any part of the server's body or clothing, or by a doubles partner. And as soon as the ball has been tossed, the free arm must be moved out of the space between the ball and the net. The ball has to bounce once on the server's side and once on the receiver's; if it clips the net and still lands correctly, it is a let and is replayed.

The last clause is the one that caught Yokotani. "It is the responsibility of the player to serve so that the umpire or the assistant umpire can be satisfied" that the serve is legal. If either official is unsure, they may warn the player once in a match without penalty; after that, the law says, any serve "which is not clearly legal shall be considered incorrect", which means a point to the opponent. The burden sits with the server. An official who is merely unconvinced is enough, which is why a player can be faulted for a serve that looked fine to him. Only for a player with a physical disability may the umpire relax the requirements.
## Why the serve matters so much

A serve opens every point, and since 2001 each player serves two points in a row before the serve passes across. Before then, under 21-point games, it changed every five. At 10-10, deuce, it alternates on every point until someone leads by two. Eleven's count of this year's results shows how often the game comes down to those few serves.

Across 26,102 games in 6,779 senior singles matches at WTT and ITTF events in 2026, team rubbers included, the average game lasted 18.4 points, so each player served about nine times. Almost exactly three games in 10 were won by the smallest margin the rules allow, two points: 15.5% ended 11-9 and another 15.4% reached 10-10 and went to deuce. In those games the server at 9-9 holds both serves that decide whether the game ends or goes on, which was Yokotani's position in Istanbul. A fault there costs more than a point.

Coaches have said so for decades. "The service is an important phase of the game, perhaps the most important, because it determines its very progress," Massimo Costantini, the ITTF's high-performance coach, wrote in an ITTF coaching article in 2020, adding that "service is a state of mind." A good serve rarely wins the point outright at the top level. What it does is dictate the first ball the server gets to attack, by disguising how much spin is on it, and which way.

The great servers made that disguise into an art. Sweden's Jan-Ove Waldner, the 1992 Olympic champion, was the model. "His strokes are a combination of the best from other players. But you cannot compare his serve to anything," his national coach, Sören Ahlén, told Sports Illustrated in 1996. "He hits with topspin, backspin, side spin or no spin and always into the corner you just looked away from."
## A century of closing loopholes

The first laws, written in 1926, the year the International Table Tennis Federation was founded and the first World Championships were held in London, said only that the server should deliver the ball "by projecting or dropping the ball by hand into the air". Players soon worked out that the hand could do more than drop it. In the early 1930s, especially in the United States, servers learned to spin the ball off their fingers as they released it, and some of the serves were close to impossible to return. The American association banned finger spin in January 1934, according to USA Table Tennis's Hall of Fame records. The Hungarian Victor Barna, five times world singles champion, urged the international federation to follow, warning that without a ban Hungary would one day send "not a team of table tennis players, but five jugglers". Finger spin was banned worldwide in 1937, in a package that also lowered the net, and the ban was in force by the 1938 World Championships.

Each later change answered a new trick. In 1947 the federation introduced the flat-hand toss, the start of today's open-palm rule. In 1967 it required the palm to be stationary and the ball to be thrown near vertically from above the level of the table, which ended serves from below the tabletop. In 1983 it outlawed stamping a foot during the serve, a noise that masked the sound of the racket brushing the ball, and stopped players serving with their back to the table. The same Congress, in Tokyo, ruled that the two sides of a racket had to be distinct colours, and in 1985 they were fixed as red and black, because opponents could not tell which rubber, grippy or slick, had struck the ball. (Since 2021 one side may be red, pink, purple or green, the other always black.) Sources date the introduction of the 16cm minimum toss differently, and Eleven could not confirm when it first appeared.

The modern rule arrived as part of the biggest reform in the sport's history. After the Sydney Olympics in 2000 the ITTF moved to a larger 40mm ball, for television, and from September 2001 to 11-point games and two serves each. The serve was next. Leading players had learned to shield the ball with the free arm or body at the instant of contact, so that the receiver could not see which way the racket moved. At its meeting in Osaka in April 2001, the federation voted for a rule that nothing could come between the ball and the net from the toss to the strike, and the vote was so lopsided that no count was taken. The rule took effect on 1 September 2002. "We want the receiver to have a fair chance to see what the server is doing when he hits the ball," Adham Sharara, then the ITTF president, said when it was confirmed.

The players' reactions that autumn were mixed. "There are some services that I'm no longer allowed to use so that reduces the effectiveness of my play when I'm serving," said Austria's Werner Schlager, who a few months later, in Paris in 2003, became the first men's world champion under the new rule. Sweden's Jörgen Persson, the 1991 world champion, worried about enforcement: "I think the new rule is not very clear." Germany's Timo Boll, then 21, thought the officials were looking in the wrong place. "I think the problem is not necessarily the free arm hiding the ball but the ball being thrown back on to the racket," he said in an ITTF press release. "I think that's the main area on which the officials need to concentrate." Maurie Poole, an Australian umpire, was more positive: "However nobody tries anymore to hide the ball with the body."
## Judging it at full speed

Persson's worry has never quite gone away. The legal and illegal versions of a modern serve differ by a few centimetres and a fraction of a second, and the umpire sits side-on at the net while the receiver looks straight at the server. Some coaches argue the rule is simply not enforced. Larry Hodges, an American coach in the USA Table Tennis Hall of Fame, wrote on his coaching blog in 2018: "We're the only Olympic sport that openly allows cheating in our sport; isn't it time we fix this?" Others point out that a strict umpire risks deciding a match on a judgment nobody can check, which is broadly Yokotani's complaint from the other side.

The governing bodies' answer has been video. The ITTF's Table Tennis Review system, which it trialled again at the Mixed Team World Cup in December 2024, lets players challenge calls on edge balls, net serves and "service compliance issues such as toss height, angle, and ball visibility". It has already been used on the serve itself. At the 2025 World Championships in Doha, India's Manush Shah had a serve called as hidden against Félix Lebrun, and the replay showed his head had blocked the Frenchman's view of the ball at the moment of contact. Review is not used at every event, though, and Yokotani's complaint was as much about the explanation he was given as about the call.

That leaves the newer fan with a useful thing to watch at Muscat this week and at the [WTT Finals in Hong Kong](/events/wtt-finals-hong-kong-2026.html) next month. Look at the server's free hand: flat and still, then a straight toss, a little higher than the net. Watch whether the free arm drops away as the ball goes up, and whether the receiver can see the ball when the racket meets it. Then watch the umpire. A century of rules has tried to make the serve fair without making it dull, and every few years a player finds the gap between what the law says and what an official can see in half a second. Waldner used it to serve into the corner you had just looked away from. Yokotani, on Thursday, found it from the other side.

charts.note: Eleven classified the final score of all 26,102 games in the 6,779 men's and women's senior singles matches (team rubbers included) at WTT and ITTF events in its results database from 1 January to 17 November 2026; walkovers and incomplete scores were left out.
